b: Typically, when I hear complaints about a pedal tuner, it’s because a player can’t see it in the daylight or it mysteriously switches modes at the worst possible moment. It’s less often that I hear complaints about lack of accuracy. But maybe that’s because players don’t know what they’ve been missing. So MXR’s new Turbo Tuner, which is effectively an evolution of Sonic Research’s much-loved Turbo Tuner, may find a lot of players celebrating the solution to a problem they didn’t even know they had. Like any good stroboscopic tuner, the MXR Turbo Tuner is simply more accurate and fluid. And that could change the way you hear your rig—and the confidence with which you use it.

If you’ve only ever used a conventional digital tuner, you might find a stroboscopic unit like the Turbo Tuner counterintuitive. Primarily, that’s because a stroboscopic tuner’s readout is almost always in motion—even when it’s practically dead on. A typical digital tuner may look accurate when its LED needle registers straight-up, but it’s only reporting an approximation. (This is true of some strobe tuners too.) MXR Turbo Tuner’s readout stays in motion because it reads and reports the wave form or tone cycle pitch in real time. This is why most guitar techs use stroboscopic tuners rather than their digital counterparts.

For newbies, this process can feel a little like learning a new language. It takes practice, and I don’t think it’s any accident that MXR’s video manual for the Turbo Tuner is 28 minutes long. New approaches and processes often require much reassurance, after all. There’s also the matter of bass and customizable tunings, the ability to adjust reference tones, and more. These are useful parts of the Turbo Tuner’s makeup that enhance its utility. But you do not need to dive deep into these functions for the Turbo Tuner to make a world of difference. And as you learn to trust the interface between your eyes and ears, deciphering the Turbo Tuner’s readout becomes second nature in a way that could come to make onstage tuning a lot less disruptive to the act of performing.
